fields.why:
In BICAR-ICU (2018) bicarbonate gave no overall benefit; the
pre-specified subgroup with pH ≤ 7.2 plus AKI stage 2–3 showed a
signal of lower mortality and less dialysis. That subgroup
became the SSC 2021 suggestion, kept in SSC 2026 (very low certainty). BICARICU-2 (JAMA 2025, n = 627,
pH ≤ 7.20 + AKI 2–3) then tested it directly: 90-day mortality
62.1% vs 61.7% (no benefit); only less kidney replacement
therapy (35% vs 50%). Bicarbonate also
makes CO2 (needs ventilation), lowers ionised calcium
and can worsen intracellular acidosis.

**Enteral within 24–48 h · hypocaloric week 1 · protein 1.2–2.0 (ASPEN) / 1.3 (ESPEN) g/kg**

a **Within 24–48 h** once haemodynamically stable — low or stable vasopressor doses are not a contraindication.
b Energy in week 1: **12–25 kcal/kg/day** (ASPEN 2022), full target ~25 kcal/kg later. Protein **1.2–2.0 g/kg/day** (ASPEN) or **1.3 g/kg/day reached progressively** (ESPEN 2023). Avoid early high protein: EFFORT Protein (≥2.2 g/kg) no benefit, possible harm with AKI or high SOFA; PRECISe (2.0 vs 1.3) worse functional recovery.
c **Hypocaloric** early (≤ 70% of target), reaching 80–100% after day 3.
d Only if enteral feeding falls short by **day 4–7** (ESPEN 3–7; ASPEN 7).

**NAC (proven in paracetamol; early-grade non-paracetamol) · Na 145–155 · CRRT for ammonia**

a **N-acetylcysteine**: proven in paracetamol ALF. In adult non-paracetamol ALF it improves transplant-free survival **only in coma grade I–II** (52% vs 30%); no benefit in grade III–IV and no overall survival benefit (Lee 2009). Paediatric non-paracetamol ALF: no survival benefit and lower 1-year transplant-free survival (35% vs 53%), worst under 2 years (Squires 2013).
b Hypertonic saline to **Na 145–155** (not 155–160); mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg if ICP rises.
c Early **CRRT** to clear ammonia; intubate grade III–IV for airway protection.
d **No** — only for bleeding or procedures (INR is a prognostic marker).

fields.a:
Range 0 to 24. Higher scores predict higher mortality: an initial or highest SOFA **above 11** (or a mean above 5) carries mortality **above 80%** (Ferreira, JAMA 2001). A SOFA that rises over the first 48 h means mortality of at least 50%, whatever the start. These bands come from the original SOFA, not SOFA-2.
**Sepsis-3**
Sepsis = suspected or documented infection PLUS an acute rise in SOFA of 2 or more points from baseline.
Septic shock = sepsis PLUS a vasopressor requirement to keep MAP at 65 mmHg or above PLUS lactate above 2 mmol/L, both persisting after adequate fluid resuscitation.

fields.a:
Map the same 3 situations to their NON-PARAMETRIC equivalent test.
**Situation** | **Non-parametric test**
Single group (paired) | **Wilcoxon signed-rank** (numbers) · McNemar's test (categories)
Two independent groups | **Mann-Whitney U** (numbers) · Chi-square test (χ²) (categories)
Three or more groups | **Kruskal-Wallis** (numbers) · Chi-square / chi-square for trend (categories)
- Non-parametric tests are used for QUALITATIVE data, or for
quantitative data that is NOT normally distributed.
fields.watch:
The non-parametric twins of the t-tests are Wilcoxon signed-rank (paired) and
Mann-Whitney U (unpaired). McNemar and chi-square are for CATEGORIES: McNemar
when the same subjects are measured twice, chi-square for independent groups.

a 1400–1500 mmol/day; cleared by the **liver and kidneys**.
b In septic shock mostly **adrenergic (beta-2) aerobic glycolysis** (driven by the Na/K pump), PLUS **reduced clearance** by the liver; tissue hypoxia with anaerobic glycolysis is only one contributor (more so in low-flow shock).
c **2 mmol/L** (part of the septic shock definition).
d A falling lactate means reperfusion and is linked to lower mortality in every patient group, whatever the starting value; a persistent rise means poor outcome. Changes are slow, so measure every **1–2 hours**.

**Classic wet & cold** | **Norepinephrine** (first line); inotropic agent | **Low CI, high SVR**. Norepinephrine is preferred: in SOAP II's cardiogenic-shock subgroup dopamine gave more arrhythmias and higher mortality, so it is not an equal choice (2017 AHA table listed both). Add inotrope once stable and **after revascularisation**

fields.a:
**2 mL x body weight (kg) x %TBSA, titrated to urine output.**
Current ATLS guidance favours starting at this lower volume - rising to 4
mL/kg/%TBSA for high-voltage electrical injury (target urine 75–100 mL/h until it clears) - and titrating the infusion
rate against measured urine output, rather than infusing the full classic 4
mL/kg volume regardless of response.
The change reflects concern about fluid creep: over-resuscitation with the
classic formula driving massive oedema, abdominal compartment syndrome
and worse respiratory outcomes.
Either version's calculated volume is only a starting estimate. The actual
infusion rate is adjusted hourly against the patient's urine output.

fields.a:
- **Permissive hypotension**: SBP **80–90** (MAP **50–60**), normal mentation, palpable pulses, until bleeding is controlled; follow lactate and ScvO₂.
- **Not in TBI or spinal cord injury**: keep **MAP 80 or more** if GCS 8 or less.
- **Restrict crystalloid**: big volumes worsen bleeding (dilution, clot disruption), oedema, hepatocellular injury.
- **Haemostatic resuscitation**: blood products first, **RBC:FFP:platelets about 1:1:1**.
Penetrating torso: restrictive policy (SBP 60–70) lowers bleeding and 28-day mortality.

- b **rFVIIa**: off-label; no outcome benefit; thrombosis; status unclear (notes); last resort only *(standard teaching, not in your notes)*.

fields.a:
**First 24–72 h**: **Gram-positive** skin flora (Staph, Strep).
**Beyond 72 h**: **Gram-negatives**: **Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter**, Enterobacterales.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics → **fungi** (including filamentous) and MDR organisms.
**Leucocytosis** early (24–48 h), then **leucopenia**; procalcitonin only supports a sepsis diagnosis, it cannot confirm one. SSC 2026: do not use PCT to decide whether to START antibiotics; use it with clinical review to decide when to STOP.
**Systemic prophylaxis**: fewer pneumonias and wound infections but more **MRSA and MDR**: role unclear.

fields.q: **What are the elements of the VAP bundle (old IHI five, and SHEA 2022 now)?**
fields.a:
**Old IHI five:** head-of-bed elevation · oral care with chlorhexidine · stress ulcer prophylaxis · DVT prophylaxis · daily sedation hold + SBT

**SHEA 2022 (current) essential practices:**
- **Avoid intubation** where possible (HFNO/NIV)
- **Minimise sedation**; daily **SAT + SBT**
- **Early mobility**
- **Head of bed 30–45°**
- **Toothbrushing WITHOUT chlorhexidine** (chlorhexidine: possible mortality harm)
- **Early enteral feeding**

Add-on if rates stay high: subglottic secretion drainage. Stress ulcer and DVT prophylaxis are NOT VAP-prevention measures.

ENDO02B|DKA-01.src: Umpierrez GE et al., Hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report, Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275 (also Diabetologia 2024)

fields.a:
a **0.9% NaCl 1 L/h** (15-20 mL/kg).
b High or normal Na: **0.45% NaCl**; low Na: **0.9% NaCl**; both **250-500 mL/h** by hydration.
c Glucose **< 250 mg/dL** in both DKA and HHS (2024; was 200 / 300) → add **5-10% dextrose** to the saline; keep insulin running.
d **Ringer's lactate, Plasma-Lyte** acceptable; **HES not preferred**; no crystalloid proven better.
e **Haemodynamic monitoring and pressors**, not blind fluid loading.

ENDO02B|DKA-12.src: Umpierrez GE et al., Hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report, Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275 (also Diabetologia 2024)

fields.q:
Potassium in DKA/HHS:
a The precondition
b K < 3.5
c K 3.5-5.0
d K > 5.0
e Why total-body K is low despite a high serum level
fields.a:
a **Urine output about 50 mL/h**.
b **Hold insulin**; give potassium (about **10 mmol/h**, 2024) until K > **3.5**.
c **20-30 mEq K in each litre** to keep K **4-5**.
d **No K**; recheck **2-hourly**.
e **Glycosuria washes K out**; acidosis and insulin lack shift K out of cells, so it **falls precipitously** once insulin starts.
fields.watch: Marrow's second chart uses 5.3 as the upper cut-off; the ADA 2009 flowchart uses 5.2; the 2024 consensus uses **3.5 and 5.0**. Hypokalaemia needs HDU care.

ENDO02B|DKA-13.src: Umpierrez GE et al., Hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report, Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275 (also Diabetologia 2024)

fields.q:
Insulin dosing:
a The two starting options
b If glucose falls < 10% in the first hour
c Target rate of fall
d At glucose < 250 in DKA (2024; was 200)
e At glucose < 250 in HHS (2024; was 300)
fields.a:
a 2024: **fixed 0.1 U/kg/h**, bolus optional. ADA 2009 options: **0.1 U/kg bolus + 0.1 U/kg/h**, or **0.14 U/kg/h** without a bolus.
b **0.14 U/kg IV bolus**, then continue.
c **50-70 mg/dL/h** (Marrow); if not reached, **double the rate**.
d Cut to **0.05 U/kg/h** (2024; ADA 2009 0.02-0.05) (or SC rapid-acting 0.1 U/kg 2-hourly); hold glucose about **200** (2024) until ketoacidosis resolves.
e Cut to **0.02-0.05 U/kg/h**; hold glucose **200-300** until mentally alert.

ENDO02B|DKA-15.src: Umpierrez GE et al., Hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report, Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275 (also Diabetologia 2024)

fields.a:
a **β-hydroxybutyrate < 0.6 mmol/L** and **venous pH ≥ 7.3 or HCO3 ≥ 18** (2024); do not use the anion gap or urine ketones.
b **0.5-0.8 U/kg/day**.
c **Home insulin dose**.
d **1-2 h** after the first SC dose (Marrow text: 2 h).
e Electrolytes, BUN, venous pH, creatinine and glucose **every 2-4 h**.

ENDO02B|DKA-16.src: Umpierrez GE et al., Hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report, Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275 (also Diabetologia 2024)

fields.a:
a Only if **pH < 7.0** (2024 consensus; ADA 2009 used 6.9): **100 mmol in 400 mL water + 20 mEq KCl over 2 h**, repeated 2-hourly until pH ≥ 7. None if pH ≥ 7.0.
b **Myocardial depression, cerebral vasodilation, coma**.
c **Hypokalaemia, less tissue O2 uptake, cerebral oedema**.
d **No improvement in outcomes**.

ENDO02B|DKA-17.src: Umpierrez GE et al., Hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report, Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275 (also Diabetologia 2024)

fields.a:
a **Pregnancy** and **SGLT2 inhibitors**.
b Ketoacidosis with glucose **< 200 mg/dL** (2024); about 10% of DKA. Also alcohol, liver failure, poor intake.
c Starvation ketosis gives only **mild acidosis**, without diabetes *(DocT)*.
d Give **dextrose with insulin from the start** to clear ketones *(standard)*.

ENDO02B|DKA-21.src: Umpierrez GE et al., Hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report, Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275 (also Diabetologia 2024)

a **Improve tissue perfusion**; treat the cause; correct electrolytes.
b **Volume first, then insulin**.
c **No proven benefit** from a bolus; **0.05 U/kg/h** infusion (2024; **0.1** if ketotic or mixed DKA-HHS).

ENDO02B|DKA-23.src: Umpierrez GE et al., Hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report, Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275 (also Diabetologia 2024)

fields.a:
a **More common than DKA**; mortality **5- to 10-fold** that of DKA (2024; older texts 15-30% vs 5%), higher with age and comorbidity.
b **Impaired access to water**.
c **Older, debilitated**, brought by a carer, many comorbidities, often **unrecognised type 2 DM**; onset over **weeks**.
d **Dehydration, hyperglycaemia, hypernatraemia, hyperosmolality**.
e **Feeding (PN/EN), GI bleed, PE, pancreatitis, heat illness, mesenteric ischaemia, infection, MI**.

ENDO02B|DKA-22.src: Umpierrez GE et al., Hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report, Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275 (also Diabetologia 2024)

fields.a:
a **High anion gap metabolic acidosis** (AG > 12) from **keto-acid anions**.
b **Hyperchloraemic, normal anion gap acidosis**: saline chloride plus renal HCO3 loss.
c 2024: **β-hydroxybutyrate < 0.6 mmol/L** with venous pH ≥ 7.3 or HCO3 ≥ 18; anion-gap closure (older teaching) is no longer used.

ENDO02B|DKA-09.src: Umpierrez GE et al., Hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report, Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257-1275 (also Diabetologia 2024)

a **Acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, acetone**.
b **Acetoacetate and acetone, not β-hydroxybutyrate** (needs a special assay).
c Beta-hydroxybutyrate converts back to acetoacetate, so the test **rises as the patient improves**.
d **Blood β-hydroxybutyrate** (2024: resolved below **0.6 mmol/L**); not urine ketones or the anion gap.

fields.a:
**Vasoactive + antibiotic before scope → band within 12 h → early TIPS if high risk**

**1** **Terlipressin** 2 mg 4-hourly for 24–48 h, then 1 mg 4-hourly (or octreotide 50 µg bolus + 50 µg/h) — start before endoscopy, continue 2–5 days.
**2** **Ceftriaxone 1 g/day** (up to 7 days) — ↓ infection, rebleeding and death.
**3** **Restrictive transfusion** (Hb 7); avoid FFP.
**4** **Endoscopic band ligation within 12 h**.
**5** **Pre-emptive TIPS within 72 h** (ideally < 24 h) for Child C 10–13, Child B > 7 with active bleeding, or HVPG ≥ 20 mmHg.
**6** Uncontrolled → covered oesophageal stent (preferred) or balloon tamponade (≤ 24 h) as bridge to rescue TIPS.

HY6|GIN-09.src: Garcia-Tsao G et al., Hepatology 2017;65:310 (AASLD); Pfisterer N et al., World J Hepatol 2021;13:731 (Table 2, adapted from Baveno VI and AASLD) · Baveno VIII Faculty (Berzigotti A et al.), J Hepatol 2026, doi:10.1016/j.jhep.2026.07.030 (statement 5.31); García-Pagán JC et al., NEJM 2010;362:2370 · Baveno VIII Faculty (Berzigotti A et al.), J Hepatol 2026, doi:10.1016/j.jhep.2026.07.030 (statement 5.35)

fields.a:
**Restrictive transfusion, early endoscopy — don't wait to fix the INR**

a **Hb 7–8 g/dL** — over-transfusion raises portal pressure.
b **Early endoscopy** (within 12 h variceal / 24 h non-variceal).
c Stop warfarin; **no routine FFP** (the cirrhotic INR does not predict bleeding); **PCC + low-dose vitamin K** only if unstable; don't delay endoscopy for INR.
d **No** — count is normal.
e Glasgow–Blatchford 0–1 = outpatient; shock index ≥ 0.9 = massive bleed; lactate above 2.5 = higher risk.

HY6|GIN-08.src: Gralnek IM et al., Endoscopy 2021;53:300 (ESGE); Baveno VIII Faculty, J Hepatol 2026 (statement 5.23)

fields.a:
**SUP only while risk persists · mobilise when the safety screen is passed**

a **Coagulopathy, shock, chronic liver disease** (SCCM/ASHP 2024; ventilation alone is not a firm risk factor). Older lists: ventilated above 48 h, TBI/burns, prior GI bleed. **PPI (e.g. esomeprazole)** or H2RA, **enteral or IV — whichever is feasible**.
b When risk factors resolve — **never continue it after ICU discharge** (↑ C. difficile, pneumonia).
c **Progressive assisted mobilisation** (sit, stand, march). Passive range of motion is for sedated/unstable patients.
